text: Regression can describe a relationship, but an observational dataset can never fully rule out confounders. A randomized experiment can. An A/B test randomly splits users into a control group and a treatment group, changes one thing for the treatment group, and compares an outcome. Because chance alone decides who sees what, the groups are comparable in everything except the change — that's what earns the word cause.

Most of the hard work happens before any data arrives. The design checklist starts with a hypothesis and one primary metric, picked first, so you can't go hunting through many metrics afterward. Next, the unit of randomization — usually the user, not the page view, so one person is never in both groups.

Then the significance level, power, and minimum detectable effect — typical choices are alpha 0.05 and power 0.80, with the MDE being the smallest lift worth caring about, like moving conversion from 10 to 12 percent. Finally, sample size and duration, fixed in advance — decide when you'll stop before you start.

Randomization is what turns a comparison into an experiment. In production you often hash the user ID so a returning user always sees the same variant. Shuffling a balanced list of labels with numpy guarantees equal group sizes, with no user characteristic influencing the assignment at all.

Suppose the baseline conversion is 10 percent and we care about detecting a lift to 12 percent. The standard formula for a two-sided test on two proportions says we need about 3,841 users in each group, roughly 7,700 total. With 1,500 eligible users per day, that's about 6 days — though in practice, run for at least one or two full weeks so weekday and weekend behavior are both represented.

The formula's denominator contains the squared difference, so halving the effect roughly quadruples the sample. At the same 10 percent baseline: detecting a move to 11 percent needs 14,751 per group; to 12 percent needs 3,841; to 15 percent needs just 686. This is why the minimum detectable effect is a business decision as well as a statistical one.

You can trust a design more when you simulate it. Running 2,000 fake experiments where the true rates really are 10 and 12 percent, the test detects the difference about 80.5 percent of the time — exactly the power we designed for.

Repeating the run with both groups at 10 percent — an A/A test — about 5 percent of runs are still called significant. That's the false-positive rate you accepted with alpha 0.05, and a real A/A check on live traffic is also a great way to catch broken randomization or tracking before it costs you.

Three guardrails: don't stop early because the result looks good — peeking inflates false positives, as Lesson 31 shows. Track guardrail metrics, like page load time or refund rate, so a win in the primary metric doesn't hide damage elsewhere. And avoid changing the design mid-test.

To recap: a good A/B test is decided in advance — one primary metric, a randomization unit, alpha, power, an MDE, and a fixed sample size. Random assignment supplies the causal claim, and the sample size formula tells you what that claim costs. Simulate to confirm, then run the test and analyze it, which is exactly the next lesson.
